After the cable cars were electrified in 1898, Walnut Hills grew as commuters shopped at Peebles Corner. Early 1900s mixed-use buildings with shops below and apartments above led to the area’s 1985 historic designation.

Founded in 1829, Lane Theological Seminary opened in Walnut Hills with support from the Lane and Kemper families. Led by Lyman Beecher, it educated Presbyterian ministers until merging with McCormick Seminary in 1932; the Stowe House remains.

Harriet Beecher Stowe lived in Cincinnati from 1832–1850, where firsthand exposure to slavery and personal loss inspired Uncle Tom’s Cabin (1852). The novel galvanized the anti-slavery movement and made her a leading American author.

Walnut Hills’ Manse Hotel, founded by Horace Sudduth in 1931, served Black travelers and social life through segregation and appeared in the Green Book. Sudduth, a Pullman porter turned entrepreneur, strengthened housing, business, and civic institutions.

For over a century, the Cincinnati Federation of Colored Women’s Clubs has advanced Black education and social welfare. Its 1925 Samuel Hannaford–designed clubhouse housed meetings and young women during the Great Migration and remains active today.
